title: JOHN THE BAPTIST WORE CAMEL HAIR AND ATE LOCUSTS AND WILD HONEY—BUT THE STRANGEST THING ABOUT HIM WASN’T WHAT HE ATE
paragraphs: JOHN THE BAPTIST WORE CAMEL HAIR AND ATE LOCUSTS AND WILD HONEY—BUT THE STRANGEST THING ABOUT HIM WASN’T WHAT HE ATE

The wilderness prophet looked nothing like the kind of man the world would follow. Yet entire crowds walked into the desert to hear him—and what he said there still confronts every comfortable Christian today.
There is something almost unsettling about John the Baptist.
Not because he was evil.
Because he was free.
Free from the desperate need to impress people.
Free from the addiction to comfort.
Free from the exhausting performance of trying to look important.
Free enough to stand in a wilderness wearing camel hair, eating locusts and wild honey, and tell religious people something they desperately did not want to hear:
Repent.
Then, when the crowds began gathering around him, John did something even stranger.
He refused to make himself the center of the story.
Think about that.
People were leaving Jerusalem.
They were walking into the wilderness.
They were listening.
Confessing.
Being baptized.
John finally had what so many human hearts secretly crave—attention.
Influence.
A platform.
A following.
And instead of building a kingdom around his own name, John pointed beyond himself toward Someone coming after him.
Toward Jesus.
That may be the most uncomfortable part of his story.
Because camel hair is easier to talk about than surrender.
Locusts are easier to debate than repentance.
Wild honey is easier to study than asking whether Jesus Christ truly has first place in our lives.
Matthew gives us one of Scripture’s most unforgettable descriptions:
“And the same John had his raiment of camel's hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins; and his meat was locusts and wild honey.”
Matthew 3:4, KJV.
The Greek is even more vivid:
“Αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ Ἰωάννης εἶχεν τὸ ἔνδυμα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τριχῶν καμήλου καὶ ζώνην δερματίνην περὶ τὴν ὀσφὺν αὐτοῦ· ἡ δὲ τροφὴ ἦν αὐτοῦ ἀκρίδες καὶ μέλι ἄγριον.”
The key words are wonderfully ordinary.
“τριχῶν καμήλου” — trichōn kamēlou — hair of a camel.
“ἀκρίδες” — akrides — locusts.
“μέλι ἄγριον” — meli agrion — wild honey.
Matthew is not trying to make John sound fashionable.
He is painting a prophet.
And suddenly an older biblical figure begins appearing in the shadows.
Elijah.
Centuries earlier, Elijah was recognized by a striking description involving a hairy garment and a leather belt around his waist.
John appears in the wilderness dressed in a way that deliberately echoes that prophetic world.
This matters because John was not merely an eccentric man who happened to enjoy wilderness cuisine.
His entire life had become a signpost.
His clothes preached.
His location preached.
His simplicity preached.
His voice preached.
But none of those things were the destination.
Jesus was.

Even John's food has sometimes been softened by modern readers because eating insects sounds strange to many cultures today. Some have suggested that the “locusts” were something plant-based, sometimes associated with carob.
But the straightforward reading of the Greek is exactly what generations of translators have understood it to mean:
Locusts.
And this was not contrary to the Torah.
Leviticus 11:22 explicitly permits certain kinds of locusts and related insects as food.
John was not violating God's Law by eating them.
He was living simply in the wilderness.
Locusts.
Wild honey.
Camel hair.
A leather belt.
No palace.
No luxury wardrobe.
No banquet table.
And yet Jerusalem came looking for him.
There is something painfully beautiful about that.
Because we live in a world constantly teaching us that before anyone will listen, we must become impressive.
Look successful.
Build the image.
Polish the appearance.
Gain followers.
Become desirable.
Protect the brand.
John walked into history looking like a man who had forgotten the entire rulebook of human approval.
And people came.
Why?
Not because camel hair possesses spiritual power.
Not because poverty automatically makes someone holy.
Not because eating unusual food brings a person closer to God.
Christianity is not a costume.
You could dress exactly like John and remain desperately far from John's God.
You could eat locusts every morning and never repent of one sin.
The power was never in the wardrobe.
The power was never in the diet.
The power was in the message God entrusted to him.
“Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.”
That is where this story stops being ancient history.
Because John is suddenly standing in front of us.
And his question is no longer, “Would you eat locusts?”
The question becomes:
What owns you?
What would become of your faith if nobody applauded it?
Would you still follow Christ if obedience cost you popularity?
Would you still tell the truth if truth made you inconvenient?
Would you still worship if God stripped away the comforts you quietly began confusing with His goodness?
Would Jesus still be enough?
That question hurts.
Especially when faith has slowly become comfortable.
There is a version of Christianity that can learn how to look alive while becoming spiritually numb.
We know when to say “Amen.”
We know which verse to post.
We know which worship song makes us emotional.
We know how to appear strong when somebody asks how we are doing.
Meanwhile, behind the polished profile picture, there may be anger we refuse to surrender.
Pornography nobody knows about.
Bitterness we have renamed “boundaries.”
Pride disguised as discernment.
Greed disguised as ambition.
Gossip disguised as concern.
Secret compromise.
A prayer life that has almost disappeared.
A Bible gathering dust while our phones receive hours of our attention.
And perhaps most frightening of all…
we can become comfortable with it.
Then John walks out of the wilderness.
Camel hair rubbing against his skin.
Leather around his waist.
The taste of wild honey lingering in his mouth.
And he does not tell us to improve our image.
He says:
Repent.
The Greek word Matthew uses is “μετανοεῖτε” — metanoeite.
It carries the call to change one's mind, to turn, to undergo a fundamental reorientation.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It is not self-hatred.
It is not theatrical guilt.
It is turning from sin toward God.
And John was preparing people for Someone infinitely greater than himself.
This is where the wilderness begins pointing toward grace.
John knew he was not the Savior.
He never claimed to be.
When Jesus came toward him, John eventually gave us one of the clearest summaries of his entire ministry:
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
John 3:30.
Read that slowly.
“He must increase.”
Not my reputation.
Not my platform.
Not my comfort.
Not my applause.
Christ.
And that may be the sentence our generation desperately needs.
Because many of us have spent years asking Jesus to increase our plans while John was calling us to decrease before His glory.
We ask God to bless our kingdoms.
John points to God's King.
We ask Jesus to make our names known.
John spends his ministry making Jesus known.
We obsess over who notices us.
John essentially says:
Stop looking at me.
Look at Him.
Then comes the moment everything in John's life has been preparing for.
Jesus approaches.
And John sees Him.
The wilderness preacher who has spent his life telling people to prepare suddenly looks at Christ and declares:
“Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.”
John 1:29.
There.
That is the heart of everything.
Not camel hair.
Not locusts.
Not honey.
Not John.
The Lamb.
Jesus Christ.
The Son of God.
The One John was preparing people to receive.
The One who would go to the cross.
The One who would bear sin.
The One who would rise from the grave.
The One whose sandals John considered himself unworthy to carry.
John could call people to repentance.
But John could not die for their sins.
John could baptize them in the Jordan.
But John could not cleanse the human heart by his own blood.
John could expose sin.
Only Jesus could save sinners.
And maybe that is exactly why this strange wilderness story matters so much.
Because some people reading this are carrying things nobody knows about.
You love Jesus…
but something has been eating away at you.
Maybe you failed again.
Maybe you promised God, “Never again,” and then did it again.
Maybe people think your marriage is fine.
It isn't.
Maybe everyone sees you serving at church, but nobody sees you crying alone.
Maybe your children think you are strong.
Maybe your parents think you are okay.
Maybe your friends believe your laughter.
God knows what happens after everybody goes home.
And somewhere along the way, shame whispered:
“You cannot come back now.”
“You knew better.”
“You've gone too far.”
“God must be tired of you.”
Listen carefully.
John's message was repentance because Jesus was coming.
Repentance and grace are not enemies.
The Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
The cross proves how seriously God takes sin.
But the cross also proves something else:
God's mercy reaches sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Jesus did not come because humanity had finally cleaned itself up.
He came because we couldn't.
That is the scandal.
Holy God.
Guilty sinners.
And between them stands a blood-stained cross where the sinless Son of God gives Himself for people who could never earn Him.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites the story of the ashamed.
He rewrites the story of the addict who finally stops hiding.
He rewrites the story of the bitter heart that learns forgiveness.
He rewrites the story of the religious person who discovers that knowing Christian language is not the same thing as knowing Christ.
He rewrites the story of the prodigal who smells like the far country.
He rewrites the story of Peter after denial.
He rewrites the story of persecutors like Saul.
He rewrites sinners like us.
Not by pretending the old pages never happened.
But by redeeming people through His grace and making them new.
Maybe you have spent years trying to edit your own story.
Delete this memory.
Hide that failure.
Crop this part.
Filter that part.
Make sure nobody sees the real version.
Jesus does something infinitely greater than image management.
He redeems.
And suddenly John's camel-hair garment begins saying something unexpectedly beautiful.
You do not have to impress the world to belong to God.
You do not need a palace.
You do not need applause.
You do not need everybody to understand your obedience.
You need Christ.
John's wilderness life was not an advertisement for misery.
It was evidence that a human life can become radically centered on a mission greater than comfort.
And yet John's story also protects us from another mistake.
Asceticism itself does not save.
John's unusual lifestyle did not make him the Messiah.
John knew that.
That is why genuine Christian discipleship can never terminate in admiration for John the Baptist.
John points away from himself.
Follow his finger.
It points to Jesus.
That is the entire purpose of the messenger.
The greatest tragedy would be to become fascinated with the man wearing camel hair while missing the Lamb of God standing in front of him.
So perhaps the question tonight is not whether you could survive John's wilderness diet.
Perhaps the question is whether there is anything Jesus has been asking you to surrender that you keep protecting.
A relationship?
A secret habit?
An unforgiving heart?
A double life?
Your pride?
Your obsession with approval?
Your need to control everything?
Your refusal to forgive?
Your fear of being completely known by God?
You already are completely known.
And still Christ calls sinners to come.
Not to remain unchanged.
To repent.
To believe.
To follow.
Grace does not merely comfort us in the prison.
Grace opens the door and calls us out.
Maybe you need to stop pretending tonight.
No speech.
No performance.
Just honesty before God.
“Jesus, I have sinned.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I cannot save myself.”
“Jesus, change me.”
“Jesus, I surrender.”
Not because typing words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing the struggle into the light is where honesty begins.

And if grace has already pulled you out of places you once thought would destroy you, tell someone what Jesus has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to remind another wounded believer that the story is not over.
Not as religious decoration.
Someone may need to hear the word John thundered into the wilderness:
Repent.
And someone desperately needs to hear what John said when Jesus appeared:
Behold the Lamb of God.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as purchasing God's favor. Grace cannot be bought. Salvation cannot be purchased. God's blessing is not merchandise.
But Christians can freely choose to support ministry and help biblical content reach more people.
Use them.
Share them.
Give them to the believer who is struggling.
Send them to the person asking questions about Jesus.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is standing in a wilderness nobody else can see.
Maybe that somebody is you.
And perhaps you thought the wilderness meant God had abandoned your story.
John reminds us that sometimes the wilderness is precisely where the noise becomes quiet enough for the most important announcement in human history to be heard.
Prepare the way.
The King is coming.
And when John finally saw Him, he did not point toward himself.
He pointed toward Jesus.
So when people remember your life, may they not merely remember what you owned, what you achieved, what you wore, how many people followed you, or whether the world considered you successful.
May they remember where you pointed.
Toward Christ.
Camel hair eventually decays.
Wild honey disappears.
Crowds go home.
Platforms vanish.
Human applause becomes silence.
But Jesus Christ remains.
And perhaps the greatest life is not the life that convinces the most people to look at us.
Perhaps it is the life that leaves people unable to forget the One we pointed them toward.
When everything else in your story has been stripped away, may the last thing people can still see be your finger pointing toward Jesus.
